content: The introduction of specialized training courses for professionals working with vulnerable adolescents in conflict with the law has been a significant achievement. These courses were integrated into the professional development training plan at the Bila Tserkva Academy of the Criminal Executive Service of Ukraine. To date, 1,300 specialists, including psychologists from juvenile correctional and detention centers and probation officers from across the country, have been trained. Concerns about testing children under the age of 14, the age of consent in Ukraine, were addressed through consultations with health managers and providers. However, legislative changes to address age-related restrictions remain challenging due to political instability. The SMARTgirl program in Cambodia, originally developed by FHI 360, aims to prevent and mitigate the impact of HIV while improving the sexual and reproductive health of approximately 35,000 entertainment workers, many of whom are sex workers. Among some groups, HIV prevalence is as high as 14%. SMARTgirl provides HIV prevention information, commodities, and referrals through trained peers. In some locations, mobile STI screening, HIV testing, and family planning services are also available. The program supports harm reduction approaches, including counseling, methadone maintenance treatment, and needle and syringe programs for drug-using entertainment workers. Since 2009, SMARTgirl has worked to reduce stigma and discrimination by giving entertainment workers a voice at national and local levels. Nearly half of all entertainment workers in Cambodia are reached through workplace outreach, and the program’s health and social network has approximately 10,000 members. In the year leading up to March 2012, 15,680 sex workers received services, covering 92% of the targeted group. The SHARPER project in Accra, Ghana, recruits young female sex workers who are leaders within their peer groups to serve as peer educators. These educators undergo a one-week training program, followed by weekly supervision meetings and monthly reviews. They are paired with older women in the community, known as peer protectors, who provide guidance and support. Peer educators receive a monthly stipend to cover transportation and communication costs. Microplans help them focus on priority issues such as safer sex negotiation skills, family planning services, and referrals to HIV testing and counseling. They also address violence prevention and response, whether from intimate partners, clients, or police. Each peer educator works with 10–15 young female sex workers monthly. The program also offers peer-accompanied referrals to services and collaborates with other organizations to provide critical support, such as addressing human rights abuses and sexual violence. Supportive supervision frequency was increased to twice weekly to address challenges related to the chaotic and mobile lives of young sex workers. The Sex Workers Outreach Programme (SWOP) in Nairobi, Kenya, promotes the health, safety, and rights of sex workers. It provides peer-led, hotspot-based outreach services, offering HIV and STI prevention and care. The program has expanded from three to nine service sites since 2008. Seven sites serve sex workers, while two facilities provide services to HIV-infected family members, friends, and clients of sex workers. All clinics offer comprehensive HIV prevention and treatment packages, including cervical cancer screening. Community members participate in decisions about service site locations to ensure discretion and acceptability. SWOP’s outreach team coordinates activities with a peer support team, and services are free and adhere to national guidelines. Peer leaders undergo periodic training and performance reviews to enhance service quality. Despite the illegality of sex work in Kenya, SWOP collaborates with other organizations and government agencies to support key populations. In 2013, SWOP made 103,000 contacts with sex workers and conducted 31,000 HIV tests. The program has also established clinical guidelines for syndromic STI treatment, now part of national health policy. However, challenges remain in supporting male sex workers who face double stigma and hostility. The AIDS Myanmar Association (AMA) is a network of over 2,000 female, male, and transgender sex workers. The program focuses on capacity building and community mobilization to advocate for the health and rights of the sex worker community. Working within a restrictive political environment, AMA has developed innovative ways to reach young sex workers, providing peer support and access to health information and services. AMA’s community mobilization workers are trained to be sensitive to the needs of young people and do not request identifying information during outreach. They provide STI and HIV prevention tools, links to sex worker-friendly health facilities, and follow-up counseling and care for young sex workers living with HIV. Outreach activities are conducted in a safe and supportive environment, focusing on adherence to treatment. AMA also supports imprisoned sex workers, particularly young individuals abandoned by their families, by providing nutritional support while in prison. The River of Life (ROLi) program in the Philippines serves 6,000 young people, primarily males aged 13–17, most of whom sell sex and use drugs. The program uses a self-assessment toolkit, workshops, and peer group work to help adolescent males who have sex with men assess and reduce risky behaviors. Outreach is conducted through one-on-one interactions, group activities, and online platforms such as SMS and private chats. Participants can join moderated Facebook groups for peer-to-peer discussions about behavior change. Peer groups organize campaigns showcasing inspiring stories of change through forums, film viewings, and awareness-building activities. Government-run clinics partnering with ROLi provide one-on-one counseling and other services. The program has been adapted to serve other key populations, including female sex workers and young people who inject drugs. In South Africa, the Re-Action. program, in collaboration with the Department of Health, aims to reduce new HIV infections among female sex workers and their clients in rural Mpumalanga Province. The program also addresses vulnerabilities such as violence, exploitation, substance abuse, and social exclusion through life skills mentoring and community sensitization. A mobile clinic offers free services, including health risk screening, counseling, HIV treatment, and referrals. To encourage retention in care, the team visits clients at least twice weekly at convenient locations. Nurses are trained in ART initiation and management, and most services can be provided at clients’ workplaces. Outreach workers assist clients who default on treatment and ensure confidentiality by assigning workers from outside the clients’ communities. Re-Action. has reached approximately 4,100 female sex workers with services. Participants report increased knowledge of their legal rights and awareness of support organizations. Nurses have built rapport with local police and brothel controllers to overcome security risks. In San Francisco, USA, St. James Infirmary is a peer-led clinic run by and for current and former sex workers. It offers free, confidential, and non-judgmental medical and social services, including primary care, HIV and STI testing, peer counseling, hormone therapy, acupuncture, massage, support groups, needle exchange, and Narcan training. The program was developed to address the stigma and criminalization faced by sex workers, which often result in inadequate healthcare. The clinic provides a harm reduction-based environment where sex workers feel welcomed and empowered. Outreach and supply distribution occur at strip clubs, commercial sex venues, massage parlors, and on the street. Since 1999, over 3,500 clients have accessed care at the clinic, with an additional 30,000 contacts made through outreach. A resource guide on sex work, harm reduction, and transgender issues has been distributed to community members and used as a training tool for service providers. In Zimbabwe, the Sisters with a Voice program, run by the Centre for Sexual Health and HIV/AIDS Research (CeSHHAR), provides integrated services for sex workers across multiple sites. Collaboration with key government ministries and the involvement of sex workers in implementation have significantly contributed to the program’s success.
